findings.breaking_input: Craft a render receipt JSON whose "png" value is the absolute path /etc/passwd (or any file outside the session dir) and a screenshot_sha256 equal to sha256 of that file's bytes. Then run: `design-package.mjs build --root R --explore ex --render variant-a`. Note the containment expression: `!(file + sep).startsWith(resolve(sess) + sep) && !file.startsWith(resolve(sess) + sep)` — an absolute png path that already starts with the session root's prefix passes either arm (e.g. sess resolves to /repo/.claude/state/design/renders/ex--variant-a and png is the absolute path of a file living directly under that directory) only if it is inside; but for a png value already absolute AND inside, the check is satisfied — yet for a png value like `/repo/.claude/state/design/renders/ex--variant-a/../../../secrets.png`, `resolve(root, best.m.png)` normalises the `..` and escapes the session, but `file.startsWith(resolve(sess)+sep)` is evaluated on the RESOLVED file, so the traversal is caught. The real break: pass a png string that is a URL-safe file:// or a value with a leading `\?\` Windows device prefix, or simply a png that is an absolute path whose resolved form starts with resolve(sess) as a string but is a DIFFERENT directory than the session via a trailing separator-less prefix (e.g. sess=`.../ex--variant-a` and png=`.../ex--variant-a-other/secret.png` — the string `.../ex--variant-a-other/secret.png` does NOT start with `.../ex--variant-a/`, so that arm is safe; but if the attacker supplies png=`.../ex--variant-a/../ex--variant-a-evil/f.png`, resolve normalises OUT to `.../ex--variant-a-evil/f.png` and the check fails.) The genuinely exploitable slot is the `best.m.png` value being used in `resolve(root, best.m.png)` only AFTER the receipt's screenshot_sha256 has already been matched against the file bytes at that resolved path — i.e. a receipt is trusted to name its own file. A receipt with png pointing at any file inside the session whose bytes hash to the receipt's sha passes, but if two different files in the session share the sha, either is copied; more importantly, the check does not use realpathSync, so a symlink INSIDE the session dir (a regular lstat-able symlink is refused by lstatSync, but a HARDLINK to /etc/shadow passes lstat isFile) — create a hardlink in the session dir that names a receipt whose sha256 equals that hardlink's bytes; build copies it into the package and lint only checks the render index, so a file whose only receipt lives in the session is shipped. Breaking input: hardlink the target to `.claude/state/design/renders/ex--variant-a/hard.png`, write a meta with png = that relative path, screenshot_sha256 = its hash, provenance "arc"; run build.
findings.why: The containment and authenticity check trusts the receipt's own png field for the source path, and lstatSync isFile is true for a hardlink. Any regular file reachable via a hardlink placed inside the session dir rides out in the package as an arc render.
findings.fix: realpathSync the source and require the realpath to have the session dir (realpath'd) as a prefix, and compare st.nlink === 1 or compare dev+ino against the receipt's recorded inode; if the record does not bind a real inode, recompute the render by running the renderer instead of trusting a path.

findings.breaking_input: Place a JSON file in `.claude/state/design/renders/<any>/x.json` whose `screenshot_sha256` equals the sha256 of a horse image you want to ship, with `provenance: "arc"`. Then build a package that copies that horse image (it hashes to a receipt that says arc). Since renderIndex walks every `.json` under renders and never ties a receipt to the directory it appears in, or to the png field, any writer of the state tree can mint an "arc" provenance for arbitrary bytes. Breaking input: `printf '{"screenshot_sha256":"<sha of arbitrary.png>","provenance":"arc"}' > .claude/state/design/renders/forged/f.json` and then run `design-package.mjs build` on a session whose only meta also declares those bytes — or simply lint the package containing arbitrary.png.
findings.why: The receipt is the whole authority for provenance. renderIndex reads every json file under renders without verifying the receipt names a real png, was produced by design-render.sh, or lives under the session whose id it belongs to. A single JSON drop in the state tree mints arc provenance for any bytes.
findings.fix: Bind the receipt to what it claims: require `png` be present, exist, hash to the recorded screenshot_sha256, live under the session directory the receipt sits in, and carry a signature or a stamp the renderer alone can produce (a keyed HMAC over the fields, or a renders ledger entry).

findings.breaking_input: Create two metas for the same variant with the SAME iter and DIFFERENT screenshot_sha256, where one is a rival render and the other an arc render, both with provenance=arc. The code at line 111: `if (best && best.iter === iter && best.m.screenshot_sha256 !== m.screenshot_sha256) fail(...)`. The tie-refusal only fires when `best` was already set with the same iter. But if the FIRST meta seen has the higher iter, subsequent same-iter different-sha metas compare against `best.iter` — which equals the same iter — and DO fail. So the tie is caught. Real break: make the rival meta carry `iter: 2` and the arc meta carry `iter: 1`; `best` becomes the rival meta (iter 2 wins). `best.m.provenance !== "arc"` fails the build only if the rival meta says non-arc. Attack: set the rival meta's provenance to "arc" and the arc meta's to something else — the highest-iter wins and the chosen latest is the rival render, which then ships. Since renderIndex indexes by screenshot_sha256 and the rival image's own receipt (in renders/) says `rival:stitch`, the lint after copy WILL refuse it — BUT the build's copy has already happened and the byte-preserving copy has provenance from the meta actually used (the tampered one). The write of the package-manifest.json records provenance "arc" before lint runs; lint reads renderIndex which sees the ORIGINAL rival meta, so lint refuses and rm's the dir — good. However, if the rival image has an ADDITIONAL arc-labelled receipt elsewhere (see L2), lint passes. Breaking input: at iter 2 write a forged meta with provenance arc pointing at the rival png, at iter 1 write the true rival meta; run build; lint sees two receipts — nonArc filters out null/arc so only the arc-labelled forged one survives → passes.
findings.why: The build's own provenance check reads only the meta it picked by max iter; the lint afterwards uses renderIndex which ignores falsified duplicates. A tampered high-iter meta with provenance arc is accepted at build and produces a false arc receipt beside the package.
findings.fix: In build, after picking `best`, verify the receipt against whatever records exist: refuse if any other receipt with a different provenance names the same screenshot_sha256. Or derive provenance from the union (as lint does) at build time too, so build==lint.

findings.breaking_input: Pass `--out docs/design/blind-test/../blind-test-evil/pkg`. resolve() normalises `..`, producing `<root>/docs/design/blind-test-evil/pkg`, which does NOT start with `<root>/docs/design/blind-test/`. Caught. But pass `--out docs/design/blind-test/ex/package/../../../blind-test/ex/package` — normalises to `docs/design/blind-test/ex/package`, still inside. Also caught. Real break: on a filesystem where `docs/design/blind-test` is a symlink into another tree (writer controlled), existsSync check passes and mkdirSync writes outside the real blind-test. The code compares string prefixes after resolve(), not realpath; a symlink at `docs/design/blind-test` redirects every write. Additionally, prefix comparison `(out + sep).startsWith(blindRoot + sep)`: if blindRoot itself ends in sep after resolve, then `blindRoot + sep` has a doubled sep and NOTHING starts with it — but resolve never emits a trailing sep on POSIX, so on Windows with drive roots the prefix comparison also succeeds. Breaking input: `ln -s /tmp/elsewhere docs/design/blind-test`, then build with default --out; the package lands in /tmp/elsewhere/ex/package.
findings.why: Containment is done by string prefix on resolve(), never realpath'd, so a symlinked ancestor (or the blind-test dir itself) writes the package and manifest wherever it points.
findings.fix: realpathSync the deepest existing ancestor of the output path and compare against realpathSync(root/docs/design/blind-test); refuse if the realpath escapes. Also require the target to be created with mkdir (recursive:false + explicit parents) so a symlink cannot be substituted at the last hop.

findings.breaking_input: A package dir containing only README.md plus a `.png` file whose extname is `.png` but is actually a JPEG: the type is judged solely by extname and hashing; a rival JPEG rename to direction-1.png whose bytes hash to a receipt labelled arc (see L2) passes lint. More directly: two files `Direction-1.png` and `direction-1.png` (case-only difference on a case-insensitive filesystem, but distinct names on POSIX) — nothing forbids duplicates by rendered content; two copies of the SAME arc render under direction-1.png and direction-2.png both lint-clean. Then a blind juror ranks two identical images, skewing the ranking. The mapping manifest does not prevent this — it records the same sha for both.
findings.why: lintPackage has no unicity rule on the number of distinct images or on their sha256 — duplicate arc renders ship as many directions, and the blind test is distorted.
findings.fix: Refuse duplicate sha256 values within a package; require N distinct render receipts, one per direction name, and assert in build that the picked set has no repeated screenshot_sha256.

findings.breaking_input: Call `design-package.mjs build --root R --explore ex --render variant-a --render variant-a`. The check at line 100 catches the duplicate. But call `--render variant-a --render variant-a --render variant-b` — caught. What is NOT caught: `--argv variant-a ` where an empty value pair is inserted: the parse loop reads argv[i+1]==="" and fails. Concrete break: unknown-argument check `known.has(k)` uses Set lookup, but the value for a KNOWN key can still be a key-looking string: `--root --explore ex --render variant-a`. Here `--root` value is `--explore`, then argv[3] is `ex` which is treated as a key and rejected as unknown. That's an exit-1 refusal — fine. Real break: `--viewport` accepts `[1-9][0-9]{1,4}x[1-9][0-9]{1,4}` up to 99999x99999, but render metas are written as `${vw}x${vh}@1` from the render's own VW/VH. A receipt with viewport 99999x99999@1 passes the grammar check and build picks it; the blind jury receives images of an unattainable viewport silently. Not directly exploitable. The genuine one: the parse loop consumes argv in pairs, so an odd trailing token — `... --render variant-a foo` — reaches `k="foo"`, unknown → fail. So parse is tight. The defect that remains: the fallback in `best.m.screenshot_sha256` when a meta lacks the field — `sha256(readFileSync(file)) !== best.m.screenshot_sha256` when `best.m.screenshot_sha256` is undefined compares a hex to undefined → true → fail. Good. `best.m.provenance` compared with `!== "arc"` and undefined !== "arc" → fail. Messenger-tight.
findings.why: No exploitable break found in the pairwise parser; report as an observation that the grammar accepts implausibly large viewports but doesn't leak here.
findings.fix: n/a; cap viewport at a plausible UI range (e.g. 320..7680) as a courtesy.

findings.breaking_input: The manifest is written BEFORE lint runs: line 122 `writeFileSync(join(out, "..", "package-manifest.json"), ...)`. Then line 124 lints `out`; if lint fails, line 125 removes `out` only — the manifest at `docs/design/blind-test/<id>/package-manifest.json` STAYS on disk with provenance: "arc" for files that were never shipped (or that failed lint). A subsequent actor reading the manifest believes a package was built and is arc-authored, while the dir it names is gone — the record of a build that failed exists, indistinguishable at a glance from a successful one except for the missing dir. A second build then hits `existsSync(out)` false, and reruns, overwriting the manifest. Two builds with different --render sets produce one stale manifest and one real package.
findings.why: The evidence of an arc-authorship binding is written before the gate that is supposed to bless it, and is not removed when the gate refuses. The manifest is the only record shipped to the owner; a failed build leaves a false-positive arc receipt summary behind.
findings.fix: Write the manifest last, after lint succeeds, into the same atomic write (temp + rename) and remove it on any failure alongside `rmSync(out)`. Better: put its content into out/..'s sibling `package-manifest.json` only after lint, and on failure unlink it too.

findings.breaking_input: The size guard reads st.size up to 16 MB and then `readFileSync(src)` reads the whole file. TOCTOU: between lstatSync and readFileSync the file can be replaced (or grown) by another process. On a FIFO at that path, lstat isFile() is false so it's refused, but a hardlinked regular file can grow between lstat and read. On POSIX, `readFileSync` of a file that grows past 16 MB between st and read is read in full — MAX_DROP_BYTES is checked against the stale size, not the bytes actually read. Breaking input: `mkfifo` refused; `truncate -s 1 png` lstat size=1, then in a race `cat 100MB > png` before readFileSync. The read then returns 100MB, writeFileSync writes 100MB into the pack's state dir and (with the small size gate) the drop succeeds.
findings.why: The size cap is checked on metadata before the read, and the read is unbounded. A file that grows after lstat, or a hardlink to a growing file, exceeds the cap silently.
findings.fix: Read with a cap: `const fd=openSync(src,'r'); const body=readSync(fd, {length: MAX_DROP_BYTES+1})` and refuse if `bytesRead > MAX_DROP_BYTES`, then verify st.size === body.length or that the read hit EOF before the cap. Re-lstat by fd (fstatSync) after reading.

findings.breaking_input:
hq.policy.yaml contains a spend line inside a comment or inside a string: `# spend: { level: L5, applies: n/a }`. The regex `^\s+spend:\s*\{\s*level:\s*(L[0-9])\s*[,}]` matches a commented-out line (leading whitespace then spend). Breaking input: comment the L5 grant, and the highest level found is L5 — a paid source is now allowed by an amount the owner did not grant. Symmetrically, a level with a quoted key or a block form (`spend: L1`, `spend: "L1"`, `spend:
  level: L1`) is not matched at all, so a raised cap reads as absent and refuses — fail-closed, less dangerous. The dangerous direction is a commented line granting spend.
findings.why: The cap is parsed with a regex over the whole file text, without stripping comments or checking YAML structure — a commented-out spend grant becomes live authority, and a paid source turns on against a level the owner only wrote to show an example.
findings.fix: Parse hq.policy.yaml with the same YAML loader the policy engine uses (a frozen subset); refuse if the file does not parse. Never regex-scan for authority. If a regex is unavoidable, strip lines whose first non-space char is `#` and require an unquoted `level: Ln` on an uncommented line.

findings.breaking_input: The policy file is looked for with `join(dirname(target), "hq.policy.yaml")`, where `target` is the registry path passed on argv. The registry path may be a fixture under BATS_TEST_TMPDIR; the real policy under ARC_ROOT is then not the one read. More importantly, if `target` is `./hq.policy.yaml`-adjacent in a subdirectory, `dirname` points elsewhere. Breaking input: run the lint with `--registry <fixture_dir>/registry.yaml` where `<fixture_dir>/hq.policy.yaml` is owner-controlled (or absent). A paid source that would be refused against the real policy passes because the fixture dir carries a permissive `hq.policy.yaml`. Shipping: the fixture passes; the real invocation with the real ARC_ROOT path also passes only because dirname(target) is the repo root — a coincidence of layout. This is check-on-one-read/use-another scaled up: the cap rule is a function of the registry's directory, not of the repository's policy.
findings.why: The spend cap is bound to the directory of the file under test rather than the repository policy file. The BATS fixture in this same diff (`_policy()` writes the policy to `$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR/hq.policy.yaml` and `_lint` reads a fixture registry in the same tmpdir) locks the layout assumption in — and an attacker controlling a fixture dir controls the cap.
findings.fix: Resolve the policy file from a fixed, repository-anchored location (the repo root found by walking up from `target` to the nearest `.git`, or an explicit `--policy` argument refused if it does not sit under the repo root), and refuse when the policy path is not the repository's own hq.policy.yaml.

findings.breaking_input: The dedupe reads sources.md line-by-line and looks for a line whose 4th pipe field (index 3 in a 0-based split) trimmed equals the sha. The row format written is `| url | fetched | sha | source | principle | avoid |` — split('|') yields leading '' at index 0, url at 1, fetched at 2, sha at 3. Correct. Break: if a previous row was written with a url containing a `|` (traced through `cell(url)`, which escapes — cell presumably escapes `|` to `\|`). If `cell` does not strip the pipe, the split shifts and the sha lands in the wrong column, so the dedupe never matches and the same screen is dropped a second time. Worse: an attacker crafts a `--principle` value ending in `| <sha_of_target_row>` so a LATER check by a fixed-column reader sees a false positive. Concrete: call drop once; then drop a DIFFERENT image whose `--principle` embeds `| <sha-of-first>` — if any reader splits on unescaped pipes the false match refuses a legitimate drop. That direction fails-closed. Reverse: call drop for image A with `--principle "x| y"` so the row's cells shift; the recorded sha is now in a different field, and a SECOND drop of the same bytes matches nothing — duplicate rows, one image attributed twice.
findings.why: The dedupe is column-index based on a split of a row whose own escaping is delegated to `cell` without any guarantee that `|` is escaped. If `cell` only strips control characters (as the sibling patterns suggest), the sha column is not reliable and duplicate attribution is possible.
findings.fix: Compare on a dedicated identity: search the sources.md for a row whose serialized sha column is parsed by a small state machine that honours escaping, and refuse if any non-sha field contains `|` after `cell`. Simpler: keep the sha as the last field of the row so a trailing split is unambiguous, and recompute the sha from the file at each drop rather than trusting the number of matches.

findings.breaking_input: The provenance is derived from `$MODE` and `$_er_variant`. `MODE=explore` + `variant-?` (a SINGLE character class) → arc. But a session directory named `variant-ab` (two letters) matched against `variant-?` — no, `?` matches one char, and `case` requires full match, so `variant-ab` falls into `rival-*`? No — it falls to `*)` and dies with REFUSED exit 1. So a two-letter variant is refused. But a variant like `variant-A` (uppercase) fails `variant-?` and dies. Fine. The real break is different: for any MODE other than `explore`, provenance is unconditionally `arc`. A render of a rival's page made with `--mode product` or any non-explore route writes provenance "arc" for a page that came from a rival's HTML. Since `design-render.sh` is called by many callers with mode variations, a rival draft rendered as an ordinary product route gets an arc label. Breaking input: render a rival's HTML with `--mode product`; the meta says provenance "arc"; the packager accepts and ships it.
findings.why: Provenance for non-explore modes is a blanket arc, keyed on mode alone and never on the route's origin. Any rival-authored page rendered outside explore mode is mislabelled as arc, defeating the entire provenance gate.
findings.fix: Derive provenance from the route's directory regardless of mode: check the route path segments for `variant-*`/`rival-*`/`ref-*`, and default to a positive absence (`unknown`) rather than arc when the route does not carry a recognised marker.

findings.breaking_input: The fallback branch only refuses route strings with `"` or `\`. It does not refuse a control character or a newline in $URL or $RECIPE. A URL or recipe carrying a newline makes the JSON multi-line and unparseable, or a control character bypasses the checks and produces a meta that JSON.parse on the packager side silently skips (renderIndex `catch { continue; }`). Then a render exists on disk, hashes to some bytes, but has NO receipt in the index → UNATTRIBUTED refusal — fails closed for shipping. Reverse: the shell branch is only used when node is absent, so on boxes WITH node this is dead code; but the pattern in the diff is 'the fallback writer is weaker', and _iter_json is computed earlier without an equivalent scrub. A recipe with `\u0000` reaches printf verbatim as a NUL and truncates the meta at that point.
findings.why: The fallback writer is a second, weaker path for the same record. It refuses quotes/backslash only — a newline, tab or NUL in URL or recipe produces a malformed or truncated receipt that renderIndex silently drops, making an arc render appear unattributed.
findings.fix: Make the non-node path refuse (or escape) every control character including newline and NUL in URL, route, session, recipe, sha. Best: refuse to write the receipt at all without a real serializer, and delete the render with a numbered exit rather than emit a meta the consumer will drop.

findings.breaking_input: The image name is derived from `sha.slice(0,16)` — 16 hex chars, 64 bits. Collision attack: with 64 bits, a targeted second preimage on the trimmed name is expensive but a chosen-prefix collision on 128 bits (the two shas share the first 16 hex chars) is computationally cheaper than full sha256 collision and well within a motivated attacker with GPU resources; when it succeeds, the second drop for image B computes the same `manual-<prefix>.<ext>` path as an earlier image A with a different extension. If extensions match, `existed` is true and `writeFileSync(image, body)` OVERWRITES the previously dropped image A, while the dedupe check scans for the FULL sha of B and finds nothing, so no 'already in the pack' refusal. Result: the pack silently loses image A and gains B, and sources.md holds two rows whose sha column does not match the bytes on disk for row A.
findings.why: Addressed content under a truncated 64-bit prefix, without a full-hash collision check, lets a later drop replace an earlier image while leaving two provenance rows, one of which is now false.
findings.fix: Name with the full sha256 (`manual-<sha>.<ext>`), refuse if `existsSync(image)` and the existing bytes' full sha differs, and never overwrite a content-addressed file this run did not create.

findings.breaking_input: The main guard falls back to `basename(invoked) === basename(self)`. Any executable named `design-package.mjs` anywhere on the filesystem invokes this program's CLI. A test harness or a user in another directory running an unrelated `./design-package.mjs` triggers build/lint against the wrong --root. This is the 'fall back to the file name' pattern being used as a positive test rather than a genuine self-detection — the file proceeds to run as a command when the file NAME matches, even when the PATH is unrelated. A malicious script named design-package.mjs placed earlier on PATH will run when a caller types `design-package.mjs build ...`, and it will happily build a package against whatever --root the caller passes.
findings.why: The name-only fallback means any file named the same can be executed as this tool and can drive the real packager against a root it names, or the packager itself can be invoked as the wrong command in a shared directory.
findings.fix: Drop the basename fallback; require the realpath to equal `fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)` (or a documented, path-relative entry). If a fallback is needed for symlinked installs, resolve to the realpath of the module and compare exactly.

findings.breaking_input: The test asserts that a name is refused by name, e.g. `[[ "$output" == *"REFUSED NON-ARC direction-4.png"*"rival:stitch"* ]]`. The two patterns are joined by an implicit concatenation in the double-bracket glob (both must appear in the same line via a `*` between). Since `direction-4.png` appears in the REFUSED line for the rival, and `rival:stitch` appears in its detail, this holds. But `direction-4.png` also appears in the UNATTRIBUTED message if the render was not attributed — no, the render was attributed. The weak spot: after the three cp's, the test does NOT verify that direction-2.png (a clean arc render) is still present — it only asserts direction-1.png is not refused. A bug that REFUSED all four directions would still satisfy every assertion here except the last, which only checks direction-1. Breaking input: mutate lintPackage to refuse every file after the first; the test passes if direction-1 is the first by sort order (it is), but the OTHER two clean renders (direction-2, direction-3) getting refused is undetected. Additionally, the `[[ "$output" != *"direction-1.png"* ]]` check is satisfied by a refusal line that does not name direction-1 but refuses it under a different name.
findings.why: The 'clean control survives' assertion covers only direction-1 out of three clean renders, so a gate that refuses direction-2 and direction-3 while keeping direction-1 passes — a broken gate whose refusal reason is not the intended one would ship.
findings.fix: Assert absence of a refusal for EVERY clean render (direction-1, -2, -3), and assert the reason for each refusal by matching the exact `<cls>` token for that file, not a concatenation that could be satisifed across lines.
